name: Local Data Projects
title: Local Data Projects
answer: Local data projects have students collect their own observations outdoors, such as plants, animals, weather, or water quality, and then use AI tools to help identify species and organize the data. The idea matters because the data belongs to the students, which makes the work meaningful and teaches them that real data is messy, incomplete, and worth checking. The main decision is choosing a tool that fits each student's age.

sections.body: A local data project starts with students gathering their own observations in a schoolyard, a creek, or the sky above the school. AI tools then help with the parts that are hard to do by hand, such as identifying a species from a photo or sorting a pile of records into something a class can examine. The problem this solves is that data in textbooks can feel abstract and finished, while data students collect themselves is theirs and carries real questions. It also gives students a truthful picture of how data actually behaves, since their own records will have gaps and errors. The teacher's key choice is matching the tool to the age of the students.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom, a class might record the plants and animals in the schoolyard, track local weather, or measure water quality in a nearby creek. For students 13 and older, iNaturalist can be used to record observations, though a parent must give permission for anyone younger, and older students should set sensitive locations to obscured or private before posting because observations are public by default. For younger students, the same organization offers Seek, which identifies species without an account and without collecting personal data. Once the data is collected, students can organize it in Google Sheets and look for patterns, and AI can help a teacher suggest questions the data might answer, such as whether certain birds appear more often after rain. The text does not give separate grade bands beyond this age split between Seek and iNaturalist.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or finding for this idea beyond the mention of Figure 8.4, which shows the difference between the two tools. It rests on practice rather than research as presented here.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set by age and privacy. iNaturalist requires users to be 13 or older unless a parent gives permission, and observations are public by default, so older students should obscure or make private any sensitive locations before posting. For younger students, Seek avoids accounts and personal data collection altogether. The decisions that stay with a person are which tool fits each student's age and how to handle location information, and the teacher remains responsible for guiding students as they check messy, incomplete data.
